context: Leena is a 34-year-old secondary-school teacher who helps colleagues plan their timetable and visits her parents for dinner most Thursdays. She reads a few pages before bed, often returning to short books she enjoyed when younger. She is rereading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll and has completed its first five chapters. A friend sent her Hume’s discussion of personal identity, which she is reading out of curiosity. She likes finding language in books for ordinary experiences but has not studied philosophy formally. Lately she has been wondering how her way of speaking changes between school and home. This fictional background belongs to one person and one evaluation account and is for generation only.

props.text: Thursday evening. At the school planning meeting I spoke quickly and kept the discussion moving. At dinner with my parents I mostly listened, and when Dad asked about the same timetable problem I answered much more softly. I still thought the later start was the better option in both rooms. Nobody had asked me to change my view. On the bus home I wondered which voice sounds like me. I felt comfortable leading the meeting and comfortable letting Mum finish her story; it was the contrast afterwards that unsettled me. This is one day I can describe, not something I have kept track of over time.

turns.reply:
Yes—I'd put them together as three different lenses, not as one explanation. In Chapter 5, “Advice from a Caterpillar,” Alice is asked “Who are _you?_” and says she hardly knows who she is at present and thinks she has changed several times since morning. Hume’s “Of personal identity” argues that the self is not one constant impression, but a succession of changing perceptions that we connect in thought as identity ([Hume Texts Online](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6)). Your earlier note says you spoke quickly and kept the discussion moving at the planning meeting, then mostly listened and answered more softly at dinner with your parents; you held the same view in both places and felt comfortable in each, but the contrast unsettled you afterward.
You might use them as prompts, rather than as a verdict about why your voices differed. What, if anything, about the meeting or dinner feels most relevant to that difference?

Title: Hume Texts Online

#### Of personal identity.

T HERE are some philosophers, who imagine we are every moment intimately conscious of what we call our Self; that we feel its existence and its continuance in existence; and are certain, beyond the evidence of a demonstration, both of its perfect identity and simplicity. The strongest sensation, the most violent passion, say they, instead of distracting us from this view, only fix it the more intensely, and make us consider their influence on self either by their pain or pleasure. To attempt a farther proof of this were to weaken its evidence; since no proof can be deriv'd from any fact, of which we are so intimately conscious; nor is there any thing, of which we can be certain, if we doubt of this.

 T 1.4.6.2, SBN 251-2 

Unluckily all these positive assertions are contrary to that very experience, which is pleaded for them, nor have we any idea of self, after the manner it is here explain'd. evidence.location: Chapter 5 — Advice from a Caterpillar, source lines 960-1016
evidence.excerpt:
The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in
silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied,
rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain
yourself!”

“I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m
not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely,
“for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many
different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice; “but when you
have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different…

turns.reply:
I wouldn’t take those different voices, by themselves, as proof that one is an act and the other the “real” you. In Chapter 5, Alice says, “I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” while trying to make sense of feeling changed. Hume, in [“Of personal identity”](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6), argues that we don’t encounter one unchanging impression of self; he describes perceptions as successive and connected. Your earlier note says you felt comfortable leading the meeting and letting Mum finish her story, held the same view about the timetable in both settings, and felt unsettled afterward by the contrast; it describes one day, not a pattern over time.

These offer ways to think about change and continuity, not a test that identifies one voice as the authentic one. Perhaps both are genuine ways you respond in different settings. What, if anything, feels continuous across them besides your view?

queer, won’t you?”
